Conflicts can occur when a person must choose between alternatives.� There are three kind of conflicting situations:


Approach  Approach�is a positive (win  win) situation.� When offered two good choices, you are interested in both possibilities.�� Although this may no fell like a conflict, you still have to consider both choices and finally make a decision.� Approach-approach conflicts sound easy to solve, but often we are fearful that we may miss some important factors and take second best.��For example, one friend asks you to a big party, but the same night another friend asks you to attend a concert 200km away.� Both will be great.� Which do you choose?


The approach gradient describes the increase in the strength of the pull toward an attractive goal, the closer the individual gets to the goal.� Once you have decided on o goal, all you attention and energy is directed towards reaching that goal.

Avoidance  Avoidance�is a negative (lose-lose) situation.� When offered two bad choices, you have to choose one of them.� You will have to assess both choices carefully and pick the lesser of two evils.��For example, you have a difficult project to do for a class, that is complicated and time consuming.� You wish you could avoid it.� You other option, is to not complete the project, and risk failing the course and having to take it again.

The avoidance gradient describes the increase in strength of the tendency of a person to avoid an undesirable goal the closer they get to the goal.��For example, if you are afraid of snakes, the closer you get to one, the more afraid you will become.

Approach  Avoidance� this situation has both positive and negative values. Few choices in or lives are all good or all bad.� For example, you just took a cake out of the oven.� You want to taste it right away (approach), but you do not want to burn your mouth, so you set it aside to cool (avoidance).� These conflicts are usually much more complex, especially if they involve our personal relationships.
